title: 9 Scam Texts You'll Get This Year (I Wrote Them)

lines.text: You tap one text link, you lose your card. I wrote nine of them. Can you spot them before I tell you?
I'm Lenny. I used to send these by the million. Now I take them apart, so they stop working on you.
Last year Americans reported losing almost sixteen billion dollars to fraud. And the number one way scammers reached them? A text message.
Here's the game. I'll show you each text exactly as you'd get it. Try to spot the trick before I say it. Number nine looks exactly like your bank, and it costs the most.
Number one. The toll text.
Unpaid toll notice. You owe two dollars and ten cents. Pay today to avoid a fifty dollar late fee.

ov.msg: Unpaid toll notice: you owe $2.10. Pay today to avoid a $50 late fee:

lines.text: Why two dollars ten? Because nobody argues with two dollars. You don't call anyone. You don't check. You just want it gone.
And the fifty dollar fee makes you hurry. A small number to pay, a big number to fear. That's the whole recipe.
My best week with this one, I sent it to every number in three states with toll roads. Some people paid twice, because they weren't sure the first one went through.
But the page doesn't want two dollars. It wants your card number, your address, and sometimes the code your bank texts you next.
And the address you type in? That's useful too. Now I know where you live, and which roads you drive. That gets sold as well.
The tell. Toll agencies don't text you random links. Check your toll account by typing the address yourself.
Number two. The failed payment.
Your subscription is on hold. Your payment was declined. Update your details to keep watching.

ov.msg: Your subscription is on hold. Payment declined. Update your details to keep watching:

lines.text: I loved this one. Everybody has five subscriptions. Nobody remembers which card is on which.
And it lands on a Friday night, right when you sit down to watch something. Annoyed people don't read carefully.
And if you do update your card? I don't charge the subscription. I charge something else, somewhere else, a few days later.
The tell. The link isn't the company's real site. If your payment really failed, the app will tell you the moment you open it.
Number three. The code sent by mistake.
Hey, sorry, I sent my verification code to your number by mistake. Can you send it back to me?

ov.msg: Hey sorry, I sent my verification code to your number by mistake 🙈 can you send it back to me?

lines.text: Here's what actually happened. I typed your phone number into a login page. The site texted you a code. That code opens your account, not mine.
Send it, and I've just set up a new account in your name, or taken over one you already have. Your messages, your contacts, sometimes your money.
And it's not only strangers. Sometimes the message comes from a friend's hacked account, asking the exact same thing. Same rule. Never send the code.
People send it because it feels polite. Someone made a mistake, you help them fix it. I built half my career on people being polite.
The rule is simple. Verification codes are for you only. If anyone asks for one, for any reason, that's the scam.

ov.label: THE RULE
ov.s: A code someone asks you for is never a mistake.

lines.text: Number four. The job offer you never applied for.
Hi, we reviewed your resume. Remote role, three to eight hundred dollars a day. Flexible hours. Interested?

ov.msg: Hi! We reviewed your resume 😊 Remote role, $300–$800 a day, flexible hours. Interested?

lines.text: You never sent a resume. But somebody, somewhere, is looking for work, and they think, maybe it's the one I forgot about.
If you answer, it's the easy job scam from my first video. Small tasks, small payments, and then you pay in to unlock more.
The first payment comes fast, so you trust it. Twenty dollars. Thirty dollars. That money is a business expense for me. Your trust is the product.
The tell. Real recruiters don't text strangers with a salary in the first line. And a real job never asks you to pay.

ov.s:
A JOB THAT TEXTS YOU FIRST
= NOT A JOB

lines.text: Number five. The parking fine.
Notice. Unpaid parking fine of forty five dollars. Pay within twenty four hours to avoid court action.

ov.msg: Notice: unpaid parking fine of $45. Pay within 24 hours to avoid court action:

lines.text: Court. That one word does all my work. Nobody wants a letter from a court over forty five dollars.
There's a street version too. A fake QR code sticker glued over the real one on a parking meter. You scan it, you pay me, and you still get the ticket.
I liked the sticker because it doesn't even need your phone number. I don't have to find you. You walk right up to me.
Real parking fines come by mail or on your windshield, with a reference number you can check on the city's own website.
Quick one. If you've already spotted a couple of these, you're doing better than most. Subscribe, because every week I take apart another one.
Number six. Your account is locked.
Unusual sign in detected. Your account will be suspended in two hours unless you verify.

ov.msg: Unusual sign-in detected. Your account will be suspended in 2 hours unless you verify:

lines.text: Notice I don't say which account. I don't need to. You'll fill that in yourself, with whatever you care about most.
The page looks like a normal login. You type your email and password, and now I have them. And if you use that password anywhere else, I have those too.
Sometimes I even sent a second text. Thanks, your account is safe now. So you'd stop thinking about it.
The tell is the countdown. Real companies don't give you two hours. Open the app yourself. And please, use a different password for every account.
Number seven. The wrong number.
Hi Daniel, are we still on for golf on Saturday?

ov.msg: Hi Daniel, are we still on for golf on Saturday? ⛳

lines.text: You reply, sorry, wrong number. They say, oh, my mistake, you seem nice. And that's it. The door is open.
Sometimes they even send a photo. A nice face, a dog, a sunset. All of it borrowed from somebody else's profile.
This is the start of the most expensive scam in America. Investment scams took almost eight billion dollars last year. About half of everything.
Next week I'm doing a whole video on what happens after that first reply. Day one to day forty. For now, the tell. A stranger who keeps chatting after a wrong number wants something.
Number eight. Reply stop to unsubscribe.
Congratulations, you've been selected for a five hundred dollar reward. Reply stop to opt out.

ov.msg: Congrats! You've been selected for a $500 reward 🎁 Reply STOP to opt out.

lines.text: This one isn't even about the reward. I send it to a million random numbers. I don't know which ones are real.
When you reply, even with stop, you tell me this number is alive, and someone reads their texts. Now your number is worth more, and I sell it to the next guy.
And the reward link? Same as the others. A form, your card, your address. Nobody has ever won anything from a text they didn't expect.
The tell. You never signed up. So don't reply at all. Forward it to seven seven two six, that spells spam on a keypad, then delete it.
And number nine. The one that looks exactly like your bank.
Did you attempt a purchase of one thousand two hundred and forty nine dollars? Reply yes or no.

ov.msg: Did you attempt a purchase of $1,249.99 at ElectroMart? Reply YES or NO.

lines.text: Of course you reply no. Anyone would. That's the point. It's not a link. It's a conversation.
A minute later, your phone rings. Fraud department. Thank you for replying. We've stopped the payment, but your account is still at risk.
And now it's my bank call from video one. Read me the code. Move your money to a safe account. Install this app so we can help.
This one costs the most because you think you started it. You replied. You feel in control. You're not.
And if you ever get a call right after a text like this, that's not a coincidence. That's a team. One person sends, another one calls.
The tell. A real bank won't call and ask you for codes, or to move your money. Hang up. Call the number on the back of your card.

ov.label: WHAT TO DO
ov.s: Hang up. Call the number on the back of your card.

lines.text: So here's the one rule that beats all nine.
Don't act inside the text. Not the link, not the number, not the reply. Open the app or the website yourself. And never share a code with anyone.

items: 2. Open the app or site yourself.

lines.text: A real problem will still be there when you check it yourself. A scam needs you to act now, inside the message.
Quick recap. Toll. Failed payment. The code. The job. The parking fine. The locked account. The wrong number. Reply stop. And the fake fraud alert.
Which one have you already got this year? Tell me in the comments. I bet it's the toll one.
Got one I didn't cover? Paste it in the comments with the link removed, and I'll tell you exactly how it works.
And if someone you love taps every link they get, send them this. That's the whole job.
Trust me. I used to write all nine.
